persons.name: Anson H. Taylor

occupation.note: 'Anson H. and his brother, Charles Taylor, came in 1832.' John Bates, interviewed in 1883, remembered 'a sort of bridge built the year before by Anson Taylor across the South Branch near Randolph Street - a log-bridge, quite near the water, over which teams could pass'; Andreas dates that bridge to 1832 and credits it to Anson H. Taylor and his brother Charles. He hauled the lumber for St Mary's from the schooner to the site with his own team.

persons.note: THE MAN WHO BUILT THE ONLY BRIDGE TEAMS COULD CROSS. Andreas: the log bridge across the South Branch between Randolph and Lake 'was, prior to 1834, the only bridge across the river or its branches over which teams could pass', and its total cost was $486.20, 'of which sum the Pottawatomie Indians contributed $200'. That last clause is a documented fact about who paid for the town's first serious piece of infrastructure and it is recorded here because it belongs to the population question as much as to the bridge.

persons.name: Charles H. Taylor

occupation.note: He is named as Anson's partner on the bridge and separately in the 1833 roster as 'Charles H. Taylor, came in 1832', with no trade. The trade is read across from the joint work.

persons.note: ONE OF THE TWENTY-EIGHT ELECTORS OF 10 AUGUST 1833, listed by Andreas as 'Charles Taylor'. This project's wolf_point_tavern record has 'Charles and Mary Taylor' keeping that house from 1831 to 1833, which would make him a tavern keeper before he was anything else and gives him a named wife; the identification is not made here because the Taylor surname is carried by at least four distinct men in this parcel's sources and merging them on a forename would be exactly the error the Isaac Harmon case was avoided for. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 3 times: Poll list of the first election of the Board of Trustees of the Town of Chicago, 10 August 1833 — “Taylor, Charles” (poll_1833_026, line 47); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Taylor, Charles” (poll_1834_106, line 275); Poll list of 1835 — “Taylor, Charles” (poll_1835_079, line 366). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Taylor' agrees with the entry's forenames; 3 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json).

research_note: THE TOWN'S BRIDGE-BUILDERS, AND A CAUTION ABOUT SURNAMES. This parcel's sources carry at least four Taylors - Anson H., Charles H., Augustine D. (a separate household here) and the 'Charles and Mary Taylor' who kept the Wolf Point tavern - plus a Mary Taylor among the First Presbyterian Church's nine founding villagers and an A. W. Taylor on the 1832 militia roll. NO TWO OF THEM ARE MERGED HERE. Merging on a surname is how a documented population quietly becomes a fictional one.

old_settler_deaths.note: LATER EVIDENCE OF A DEATH, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. Fergus's 1843 directory (1896) prints an obituary list of old settlers, and one of its entries meets somebody of this name. THE HEADER OF THE LIST IS QUOTED ABOVE, and it is the limit the whole reading turns on. It does not mean the person was in Chicago in 1835, and it does not mean they arrived before 1843 — the list's own header, quoted above, says it also names citizens who arrived later and others merely 'prominently connected with Illinois history'. A match means one thing: a name in the 1835 layer and a name in this list agree on surname and first initial, and the list gives that name a death date and an age. The date and the interval are the payload. Whatever is carried is carried as evidence of a DEATH and of an interval the birth falls in, never as an 1835 fact and never as a grade. T-0513 consolidates and T-0514/T-0515 apply; this file changes no record. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. A death notice printed in 1896 says a person of this name died on a day; under the ratified ladder (T-0513) that is later evidence about a DEATH, and it is never an 1835 residence. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

people.birth_year_arithmetic: The page prints the death as 'August 3, 1892' and the age as 'aged 56'. An age of 56 completed years means at least 56 and less than 57, so the birth falls between 1835-08-04 and 1836-08-03: the birth year is 1835 or 1836. The subtraction is this project's; the page states no year of birth.

directories.note: LATER EVIDENCE, BESIDE THE 1835 CLAIMS AND NOT INSIDE THEM. A Chicago directory of 1839, 1843 or 1844 meets somebody of this name and this pass records what it prints. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry.
